scenes.tts: What happens to a brain when the nucleus cannot catch up?
scenes.visual: Title card: When the Engine Breaks. A neuron whose leading process keeps extending while its nucleus stays low in the wall. Label: schematic.
scenes.narration: What happens to a brain when the nucleus cannot catch up?

scenes.tts: Disrupt that machinery, and neurons can stall short of their layers.
scenes.visual: Many neurons stalled at different depths of the wall, short of the cortical plate.
scenes.narration: Disrupt that machinery, and neurons can stall short of their layers.

scenes.tts: One result can be lissencephaly. The cortex has reduced or absent folding. In the classic form it is also thick and poorly layered.
scenes.visual: Two schematic brain outlines: a folded cortex and a smooth, thick one. Label: lissencephaly, reduced or absent folding.
scenes.narration: One result can be lissencephaly. The cortex has reduced or absent folding. In the classic form it is also thick and poorly layered.

scenes.tts: Losing one copy of L I S one is enough to cause it. L I S one is deleted in Miller-Dieker lissencephaly.
scenes.caption: Losing one copy of LIS1 is enough to cause it. LIS1 is deleted in Miller-Dieker lissencephaly.
scenes.visual: A chromosome 17 diagram with band 17p13.3 marked. Label: LIS1, one copy lost is enough.
scenes.narration: Losing one copy of LIS1 is enough to cause it. LIS1 is deleted in Miller-Dieker lissencephaly.

scenes.tts: That deletion also removes neighbouring genes, which contribute to a more severe syndrome.
scenes.visual: The deleted segment widens to cover neighbouring genes, one labelled YWHAE (14-3-3 epsilon).
scenes.narration: That deletion also removes neighbouring genes, which contribute to a more severe syndrome.

scenes.tts: A mouse cortex is smooth to begin with. So in mice you look at migration speed and where neurons end up.
scenes.visual: A smooth mouse brain outline. Inside, layers drawn jumbled. Label: example mouse phenotype, disordered layers; loss of folds is not the readout.
scenes.narration: A mouse cortex is smooth to begin with. So in mice you look at migration speed and where neurons end up.

scenes.tts: A second gene, doublecortin, sits on the X chromosome. Its protein binds and stabilizes microtubules. Boys with a mutation typically have lissencephaly.
scenes.visual: An X chromosome with DCX marked. Doublecortin proteins clamp along a microtubule.
scenes.narration: A second gene, doublecortin, sits on the X chromosome. Its protein binds and stabilizes microtubules. Boys with a mutation typically have lissencephaly.

scenes.tts: Now a girl carries one mutant copy. Each of her cells switches off one X at random. What would her cortex look like?
scenes.visual: A girl icon with two X chromosomes, one marked mutant. Caption: Pause and predict.
scenes.narration: Now a girl carries one mutant copy. Each of her cells switches off one X at random. What would her cortex look like?

scenes.tts: She is a mosaic. Neurons using the normal copy migrate. Some using the mutant copy stall.
scenes.visual: A mosaic of two cell colours: one colour reaches the cortical plate, some of the other colour stop in the white matter.
scenes.narration: She is a mosaic. Neurons using the normal copy migrate. Some using the mutant copy stall.

scenes.tts: The stalled neurons form a band of grey matter beneath the cortex. It is called double cortex.
scenes.visual: A schematic MRI: a normal cortex with a second grey band below it. Label: subcortical band heterotopia, or double cortex.
scenes.narration: The stalled neurons form a band of grey matter beneath the cortex. It is called double cortex.

scenes.tts: A kinase called C D K five sits upstream. Its targets include doublecortin and a dye-neen regulator. Mice lacking it have disordered layers.
scenes.caption: A kinase called Cdk5 sits upstream. Its targets include doublecortin and a dynein regulator. Mice lacking it have disordered layers.
scenes.visual: Cdk5 with its activator p35 phosphorylates NDEL1 and doublecortin. Label: mice lacking Cdk5 or p35, disordered cortical layers.
scenes.narration: A kinase called Cdk5 sits upstream. Its targets include doublecortin and a dynein regulator. Mice lacking it have disordered layers.

scenes.tts: The two-stroke climb is not the whole trip. In embryonic rat cortex, newborn neurons first move to the subventricular zone.
scenes.visual: Back to the wall. Caption: Noctor, Kriegstein and colleagues, 2004, embryonic rat cortical slices. A newborn neuron moves from the ventricular zone to the subventricular zone.
scenes.narration: The two-stroke climb is not the whole trip. In embryonic rat cortex, newborn neurons first move to the subventricular zone.

scenes.tts: There they become multipolar, with several short processes. They move slowly, change direction, and make little net progress for about a day or longer.
scenes.visual: The neuron sprouts several short processes that extend and retract; it drifts a little in changing directions. A clock ticks in the corner. Label: multipolar stage, about a day or longer.
scenes.narration: There they become multipolar, with several short processes. They move slowly, change direction, and make little net progress for about a day or longer.

scenes.tts: Many then move back toward the ventricle for a time. Why some cells go back is not settled.
scenes.visual: The neuron drifts back toward the ventricle. A question mark appears.
scenes.narration: Many then move back toward the ventricle for a time. Why some cells go back is not settled.

scenes.tts: Then they turn bipolar and begin the sustained climb to the cortical plate. Now the front goes first.
scenes.visual: The neuron grows one leading process and begins the two-stroke climb: dot, then disc. Label: transition to sustained bipolar locomotion.
scenes.narration: Then they turn bipolar and begin the sustained climb to the cortical plate. Now the front goes first.

scenes.tts: L I S one matters at this turn too. So one defect can stall cells at more than one step.
scenes.caption: LIS1 matters at this turn too. So one defect can stall cells at more than one step.
scenes.visual: LIS1 tags appear at the multipolar-to-bipolar turn and at the climb.
scenes.narration: LIS1 matters at this turn too. So one defect can stall cells at more than one step.

scenes.tts: The two-stroke cycle explains one way migration can fail. When you film a migrating neuron, track the nucleus, not the tip.
scenes.visual: Closing card: Track the nucleus, not the tip. The bipolar cycle is one way neurons migrate.
scenes.narration: The two-stroke cycle explains one way migration can fail. When you film a migrating neuron, track the nucleus, not the tip.
